concept.name: Capital gain
concept.definition: The profit realized when a capital asset — such as stocks or bonds held as investments — is sold for more than its adjusted basis; per the IRS, a capital gain is the excess of the amount realized on sale over the asset's adjusted basis. Gains are classified as short-term (asset held one year or less) or long-term (held more than one year), with long-term net gains generally taxed at preferential rates.
concept.intuition: Buy low, sell high — the positive difference between what you paid (your basis) and what you sold for is your capital gain, and the tax rate depends on how long you held it.
concept.mechanics: Gain is computed per disposition as amount realized minus adjusted basis (generally cost, with adjustments). Short-term gains net against short-term losses and are taxed as ordinary income; long-term gains net against long-term losses and most net long-term gain is taxed at 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on taxable income, with special rates for collectibles and certain real-estate gain. Sales are reported on Form 8949 and summarized on Schedule D.
concept.formula: Capital gain = amount realized - adjusted basis (when amount realized > adjusted basis); long-term if holding period > 1 year, short-term if <= 1 year.
concept.failure_modes: Basis errors (neglecting reinvested dividends, wash-sale adjustments, corporate actions) produce misreported gains; the one-year holding boundary and trade-date settlement conventions cause classification mistakes, and unrealized gains create no tax event until disposition.
concept.misconceptions: A capital gain is not income received while holding the asset — dividends and interest are separate; nor are all investment gains 'capital' — dealer property, inventory, and certain hedging transactions produce ordinary income regardless of price appreciation.
concept.example: You buy 100 shares at $30 ($3,000 basis) and sell them 14 months later at $45 ($4,500 realized): the $1,500 long-term capital gain is taxed at the preferential long-term rate for your income bracket.

citations.source: IRS Topic No. 409, Capital Gains and Losses
